raw_text:
The subcutaneous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (S-ICD) was developed to preserve the survival benefit of defibrillator therapy while avoiding intravascular and intracardiac leads. Early feasibility work showed that ventricular fibrillation could be sensed and terminated using a parasternal subcutaneous electrode and a lateral pulse generator [1]. Subsequent US investigational-device and early multicentre cohorts confirmed high acute conversion efficacy, acceptable short-term safety, and the distinctive complication profile of an extravascular system [2], [3], [4]. In practice, the S-ICD is best understood not as a replacement for all transvenous ICDs, but as a complementary platform for patients who need defibrillation and do not need chronic bradycardia pacing, cardiac resynchronization therapy, or antitachycardia pacing (ATP).

Prospective registries have defined the technology’s performance across progressively more “real-world” populations. EFFORTLESS first demonstrated broad international use, with most spontaneous ventricular tachyarrhythmias successfully converted and inappropriate shocks mainly related to oversensing [5]. Pooled IDE/EFFORTLESS data supported durable safety and shock efficacy at 2 years [6]. Later EFFORTLESS analyses showed stable clinical shock efficacy through midterm and 5-year follow-up, but also highlighted generator changes, infections, erosions, and the occasional later need for pacing or transvenous conversion [7], [8]. The US post-approval registry extended these findings to a population with more left ventricular dysfunction, diabetes, renal disease, and primary-prevention indications than earlier cohorts [9], and its 1-year analysis showed low rates of inappropriate shock when contemporary programming and discrimination were used [10]. UNTOUCHED was particularly important because it prospectively studied primary-prevention patients with left ventricular ejection fraction ≤35%, using standardized high-rate programming and contemporary sensing filters; inappropriate shocks were lower than in early experience [11].

Randomized evidence has clarified trade-offs versus transvenous ICDs. PRAETORIAN demonstrated noninferiority of S-ICD therapy compared with transvenous ICD therapy for the composite of device-related complications and inappropriate shocks in patients without pacing indications [12]. Secondary analyses showed that ATP in transvenous ICDs can terminate some monomorphic ventricular tachycardias painlessly, whereas S-ICD recipients more often receive shocks for treatable sustained ventricular arrhythmias, although overall appropriate therapy outcomes were comparable [13]. Conversely, lead-related complications and invasive interventions were more frequent with transvenous systems [14]. Thus, patient selection depends on the expected lifetime risk of transvenous lead failure or infection versus the likelihood of recurrent monomorphic VT, bradyarrhythmia, or future CRT need.

Implantation requires pre-procedural electrocardiographic screening because the S-ICD senses far-field subcutaneous signals. The START study showed that S-ICD discrimination algorithms can perform well, but oversensing remains central to inappropriate therapy [15]. Contemporary filters such as SMART Pass, optimized vectors, exercise or postural screening in selected patients, and high-rate conditional/shock zones have reduced T-wave and myopotential oversensing [16]. Defibrillation testing remains more debated for S-ICD than for standard left-sided transvenous ICDs because shock vectors traverse extracardiac tissue. High-voltage impedance, obesity, posterior generator position, and lead/generator geometry influence conversion success [17]. Radiographic tools such as the PRAETORIAN score help assess implant position and defibrillation probability [18]. Technique has also evolved from three incisions toward two-incision and intermuscular generator placement, reducing discomfort, erosion, and migration in experienced hands [19], [20].

The S-ICD is attractive in young patients, those with inherited arrhythmia syndromes, limited venous access, prior device infection, dialysis dependence, or congenital anatomy in which endovascular leads are undesirable. Long-term matched comparisons suggest fewer lead-related complications but similar mortality compared with transvenous ICDs [21], and propensity-matched SIMPLE/EFFORTLESS analyses support comparable shock efficacy with different adverse-event patterns [22], [23]. In hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, where patients are often young and pacing needs are initially uncommon, early and multicentre data show effective therapy, although screening failure and inappropriate shocks remain considerations [24], [25]. Asian experience and inherited-arrhythmia cohorts reinforce feasibility but underscore the need for careful sensing assessment in Brugada syndrome and other dynamic ECG phenotypes [26], [27], [28].

Important limitations remain. The S-ICD cannot deliver chronic pacing, ATP, or CRT, and therefore is poorly suited to patients with symptomatic bradycardia, advanced conduction disease, CRT indications, or recurrent scar-related monomorphic VT likely to respond to ATP [29], [30]. Battery longevity, generator bulk, cosmetic concerns, perioperative pain, infection management, and need for future system revision should be discussed explicitly. Future directions include smaller generators, longer battery life, improved sensing algorithms, leadless pacing–defibrillator communication, and randomized data on defibrillation-test omission. For appropriately selected patients, however, the S-ICD is now a mature, evidence-based extravascular defibrillator strategy that reduces exposure to the long-term hazards of transvenous leads while maintaining effective protection from sudden arrhythmic death.
